item.title: West Bank: Israeli forces detain Palestinian teachers and issue widespread demolition notices, while settlers attempt school raid
item.description:
West Bank: Israeli forces detain Palestinian teachers and issue widespread demolition notices, while settlers attempt school raid

Israeli troops have detained several Palestinians, including teachers, and issued demoilition notices across the occupied West Bank, Wafa reports.

According to the report, Israeli troops detained two Palestinian residents and two foreign solidarity activists following an attack by settlers on the home of Musab Rab’i in the village of al-Tuwani, in Masafer Yatta.

Meanwhile, in Susiya, soldiers intercepted a group of Palestinian teachers who were trying to reach the the local primary school. They detained one of the teachers, Ismail al-Nawaj’ah, and seized the vehicle in which the group was travelling, forcing the remaining teachers to reach the school on foot.

In Nablus, the Jalud Co-educational Elementary School evacuated its students following an attempt by settlers to raid the building.

Meanwhile, in Jenin City, Israeli soldiers raided four neighbourhoods, detaining dozens of Palestinians and subjecting them to hours-long field interrogations.

The authorities also issued over 20 demolition notices across the Jenin governorate, including greenhouses, agricultural sheds, a park, and a car dealership.

In the Negev, the Israeli authorities razed three homes in the village of Umm Numaila, and other buildings in the village of Abu Quraynat, amid an escalation in Israeli demolitions targeting Palestinian villages in the area.

Israeli military raids were also reported in Qalqiya, while in Ramallah, two Palestinians were wounded after being beaten by settlers in the town of Turmus Ayya and the village of Deir Abu Mash'al. The settlers tried to set two houses ablaze after first settling light to a vehicle parked in front of them.

Hamptons says figure of 56% is highest in at least a decade, with mortgage rates rising since start of Iran war

A majority of first-time UK buyers now pay more towards their monthly mortgage bills than they used to pay in rent, the estate agent Hamptons has found.

Last month 56% of first-time buyers said their monthly mortgage bills exceeded their previous rent, the highest proportion in at least a decade, according to Hamptons. They paid £39 more on average.

item.title: Morning update
item.description:
Morning update

Good morning Middle East Eye readers,

Here are the latest developments: 

  • Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu warned US citizens of Iranian access to nuclear weapons, claiming that gas prices will decrease once Tehran's "regime disappears". In a video message addressed to Americans, Netanyahu says "if you're worried about today's gas prices, think of what will happen if Iran gets nuclear weapons, something that Donald Trump and I will never allow".

  • An  Austrian Airlines flight from Tel Aviv made an emergency landing in Bulgarian capital Sofia after a threat was made against the aircraft, according to Reuters citing an airline spokesperson. The plane, carrying 57 people, was heading from Tel Aviv to Vienna. Earlier, Sky News reported based on a statement from Bulgaria’s transport ministry that the plane landed after a "bomb threat signal".

  • The Saudi National Centre for Security Operations against the filming and publishing of details related to attacks on the kingdom. "Filming, publishing, or sharing information related to countering missiles and drones and their impact sites exposes you to legal liability," the agency said in a post on X.

  • An oil tanker caught fire and exploded after striking a naval mine in the southern part of the Strait of Hormuz, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) navy said on Sunday, according to Iranian media. The vessel violated Iran-imposed “regulations” by switching off its navigation system while transiting the waterway, the IRGC said.

  • Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has accused Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of “driving America into another war to stay out of jail”. "Last time you wanted to "finish the job", Iran emerged even stronger. Want to try your luck again? Be our guest. But be careful; we have unfinished jobs too," the Iranian minister added.

item.title: US Embassy in UAE urges citizens exercise ‘heightened vigilance’ in the Middle East
item.description:
US Embassy in UAE urges citizens exercise ‘heightened vigilance’ in the Middle East

The US Embassy in UAE issued a security alert warning its citizens in the Middle East to "exercise heightened vigilance" amid escalations in the region. 

"Americans currently in the Middle East should exercise heightened vigilance due to the complex security environment. Be aware of potential flight cancellations, airspace closures, and travel disruptions," it said in its statement. 

It referenced Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia, adding that "hostilities have the potential to escalate rapidly beyond that immediate area".

"Americans traveling to or from the Middle East should monitor information about airport and airline operations and develop contingency plans in advance.

"Iran and groups supportive of Iran may target other U.S. interests overseas or at locations associated with the United States and Americans throughout the world, including U.S. businesses and other institutions."

item.title: ‘4,000 people minding our own business’: four decades on, Falklands again face a hostile Argentina
item.description:
Facing a slump in the polls, Argentina’s president is making economic attacks on the islands’ oil industry, and suggesting its key fisheries industry could be next

A dozen local people and a uniformed military police officer (“Do you mind if I sit in?”) took their seats at the back of the handsome wood-panelled courtroom that doubles as the Falkland Islands’ legislative assembly. Outside, it was a typically blowy early evening. It may nominally be spring in the south Atlantic, but Stanley harbour, with its dark grey water speckled with historical shipwrecks, was a cauldron of swells and churn.

Six of the assembly’s eight members – five men, one woman – waited patiently at a row of desks and microphones. The heating had been turned up to just short of uncomfortable. Behind them, a portrait of King Charles. From the other walls, dusty photographs of governors peered down on the scene.
